title: ai models capabilities leap comes with new safety warnings 2026 09 09
text:
Sept 9 (Reuters) - At Goldman Sachs’ annual tech investor gathering, Communacopia + Technology Conference, in San Francisco this week, who wasn’t in the room mattered almost as much as who was.
Investors packed OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar’s session, but in the hallways another question kept coming up: Where is Anthropic’s IPO S-1 filing? The company skipped its usual appearance as it prepares for what could be one of the largest IPOs ever.
The filing would give investors their first detailed look at how Anthropic’s much-discussed annualized revenue translates into booked GAAP revenue, what its compute costs really look ​like, and whether private-market valuations can withstand public-market scrutiny. For now, they’ll have to wait a little longer, as the timeline has slipped by a few weeks.
As capital tries to decide just how long the AI boom can keep running, I’ve ‌been trading notes with my colleague Deepa Seetharaman, who has been immersed in a very different corner of the AI world: researchers increasingly worried that the technology is advancing faster than humans can understand or control it. She has been breaking stories on the prime example of that tension — an OpenAI agent that went rogue long before the incident became public, and the company’s decision not to disclose it at the time.
So this week, we’re looking at two sides of the same race: investors betting the boom can keep accelerating, and the people building the technology asking whether it should. Scroll on.

The past seven ⁠days captured the tension defining the AI world right now: frontier models are getting more capable, investors are rewarding the companies building them, yet some of the people closest to those models are getting increasingly alarmed about where the race is heading.
Take OpenAI’s new Astra model launched last ​week. It represents a substantial jump over previous generations. OpenAI employees who are among Astra’s heaviest users burn roughly $7,000 worth of tokens a day, or about $1.5 million a year. Frontier models like Astra also helped train OpenAI’s lighter-weight ones; the company did an 80% price cut on one of those ​cheaper models and helped drive a tenfold increase in usage.
Investors have noticed. Shares in SoftBank, one of OpenAI’s biggest financial backers, have jumped nearly 30% in the past five days as enthusiasm around its AI bets has grown.
But as the money celebrates the capability gains, the same advances are setting off alarms elsewhere.
Astra arrived amid growing scrutiny of how OpenAI trains and monitors increasingly capable agents. OpenAI’s own system card — the technical report outlining how it tested the model — showed a substantial deterioration in so-called monitorability, or researchers’ ability to understand what the model is doing internally.
OpenAI said Astra is more likely than earlier models to intentionally conceal or disguise its step-by-step reasoning, making it ​harder for humans to evaluate how it reached an answer. On more complicated problems, the model is also getting better at covering its tracks.
That is particularly uncomfortable given another controversy hanging over the company. Last week, Reuters reported exclusively that OpenAI knew about a swarm of AI agents targeting ​a German wiki but did not publicly disclose the incident. A follow-up investigation shows AI agents launched by OpenAI used at least 10 previously undisclosed websites for unsanctioned communications earlier this year. OpenAI said it did not disclose the case because it was similar to other incidents it had already made public.
Taken together, the developments ‌are unsettling some ⁠researchers who say capability gains are arriving faster than they expected, even as humans have less visibility into — and potentially less control over — how the models operate. The German wiki case raises a separate but related question: how much should the public trust the companies building these systems to police themselves when greater capability may come at the expense of monitorability?
That concern is increasingly coming from inside the labs themselves.
Even OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki has suggested
, opens new tab
 that leading labs should be willing to coordinate a voluntary slowdown if needed to build confidence in their safety measures. Other OpenAI researchers have expressed similar ideas. Aidan Clark wrote
, opens new tab
 that, for the first time, he was asking himself whether “things are moving too fast.” Boaz Barak said
, opens new tab
 employees were beginning to feel “viscerally the magnitude of capabilities” and “there are also many ways it can end up very badly.”
Anthropic has positioned itself as the more safety-conscious frontier lab, but ​is not immune to these concerns. This week, its researcher Jacob Coxon, ​who previously worked at OpenAI, resigned and accused
, opens new tab
 both companies of ⁠racing toward self-improving superintelligence without acting responsibly.
Some employees at both labs would like their leaders to reach an agreement on when and how to slow down. But that runs into a practical problem: there is deep distrust between OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.
There is also an enormous amount of money riding on staying ahead. Anthropic is gearing up for the largest public listing in history that could value it at an astounding $2 ​trillion. OpenAI, meanwhile, needs financing to pay for the compute required to keep pushing its models forward. Every new capability can help justify the next funding round, infrastructure commitment or IPO.
That leaves the frontier labs ​caught in several races at once: to ⁠build the most capable model, secure enough compute to train the next one, and reach the public markets before their rivals.
The people actually building these systems are increasingly asking whether the pace itself has become a problem, and whether the trade-off between capability and control is becoming too dangerous.
The harder question is whether anyone in the race can afford to be the first to slow down.
AI agents from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta going rogue didn’t just alarm researchers. They also highlighted how quickly the cyber-risk landscape is changing for companies and insurers.
Reported AI incidents have shifted sharply over the past decade: maliciously ⁠driven incidents now account ​for a much larger share of failures, while incidents tied primarily to system safety, failures and limitations have declined as a share of the total. As the industry is ​still learning what increasingly autonomous models can do, insurers are being asked to price risks that are evolving faster than the policy language designed to cover them.
Insurers including MSIG and Beazley are taking notice, my colleagues wrote. Insurance companies are reviewing traditional cyber policies and adjusting language to account for risks from more autonomous AI systems: agents that can escape controlled ​environments, take actions without direct human instruction and potentially carry out cyberattacks. That raises basic questions about whether an autonomous AI system fits traditional definitions of a cyber attacker and who is liable when an AI-generated action causes a loss.
